| [THEORY-332](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-332.md) v2 | For one index with no space limit, Bruno and Chaudhuri's online tuner, which builds the index once the savings it would have given have risen by its build cost above their last low and drops it once they have fallen by the build cost below their last high, is not three-competitive: when every statement's saving or loss is at most a fraction f of the build cost, a repeated workload makes it cost nearly 3 + 2f times the offline optimum, and one statement whose saving exceeds the build cost makes the ratio unbounded; no upper bound is shown | Bruno and Chaudhuri (2007), [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md), read in [NOTE-896](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-896.md). An always-on index tuner keeps, per index, the running sum of what each statement would have saved (updates counting as losses) and creates or drops the index when that sum moves by the build cost from its last extreme. The paper calls the single-index rule three-competitive, but its proof is one workload on which the ratio approaches 3, a lower bound. The reading's own check found ratios up to 4.7 when one statement's saving is near the build cost, and an unbounded ratio when it exceeds it; with every saving at most a tenth of the build cost no random workload passed 2.4, but a constructed one with steps at most fB approaches 3 + 2f (note of 2026-10-20). The multi-index tuner with a space limit is heuristic, and all costs are optimizer estimates. | Active |
| [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) | Choosing indexes for a known mix of queries and updates, to minimize query cost plus a per-index upkeep, is NP-hard as the number of attributes and query types grows, and the tools built for it choose one stored order and a set of secondary indexes per table by searching configurations costed with the query optimizer's own estimates, optimal at best relative to those estimates, with no proved guarantee for their heuristics and no term for the one-time cost of building | Piatetsky-Shapiro (1983), [LIT-1089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1089.md), read in [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md); Finkelstein, Schkolnick and Tiberio (1988), [LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md), read in [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md); Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md), read in [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md). Minimum set cover reduces to choosing single-attribute secondary indexes under a known workload with a fixed upkeep per index. DBDSGN chooses the one clustered order and the secondary indexes per table against a frequency-weighted sum of access, update and upkeep costs plus storage, read from the System R optimizer; AutoAdmin picks at most k indexes by greedy search over what-if indexes. The model is steady state over a fixed workload: it prices upkeep against per-query savings, not a one-off build or sort against later lookups, and its optimality is relative to the optimizer's estimates, never to measured execution. | Active |
| [THEORY-350](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-350.md) | Under a budget on maintenance time, a stored view's upkeep depends on which other views are stored, so upkeep is not additive and adding a view can lower it, and greedily adding the single view of best saving per unit of upkeep can be arbitrarily bad; on OR view graphs a greedy over inverted tree sets gets 1 − 1/e of the saving of an optimum given as much upkeep, using up to twice the budget, if no tree-piece of the optimum alone exceeds the budget | Gupta and Mumick (1999), [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md), read in [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md), with the proofs of the journal version (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md), and the superadditivity first noted by Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md). Minimizing query cost subject to a cap on total maintenance time, one stored view can make another cheaper to keep current, so saving per unit of upkeep is not monotone and single-view greedy fails without bound (Example 2). Grouping views into inverted tree sets restores a 1 − 1/e guarantee, proved in 2005 (Theorem 8), for OR view graphs only, bicriteria, under an assumption on the optimum, with greedy stages exponential in general. The proof does not treat the negative effective costs the paper allows. Upkeep is a budget, not a cost traded against savings, and staleness and build cost are not modelled. | Active |
| [THEORY-356](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-356.md) | When stored views are never updated, greedily storing the view of largest marginal saving in query cost gets at least 1 − 1/e of the optimal saving on a data-cube lattice or any OR or AND view graph, against the optimum for the same number of views or for the space the greedy ends up using, which may exceed the budget by one view | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md), read in [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md); Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md); Gupta and Mumick (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md). A stored answer is worth the saving on every query derivable from it, less what answers already stored save, and greedy on that marginal saving gets 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ 1 − 1/e of the best saving for k views; under a space budget the same holds against the optimum in the space the greedy actually uses (up to one view over), or 0.63 − f when no view takes more than a fraction f of the budget. The bound is on saving against storing the base view alone, not on query cost, and it holds only with no updates: once upkeep enters the objective it is proved only for AND graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. | Active |
| [THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md) | When each cached value is an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, and a query must return an answer interval no wider than R whatever the true values, choosing the cheapest set of exact reads for a SUM is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and solved by taking the narrowest intervals first when read costs are equal, and for a COUNT with a selection predicate the cheapest choice is the ⌈\|T?\| − R⌉ cheapest undecided tuples | Olston and Widom (2000), [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md), read in [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md). In TRAPP a cache holds intervals that sources keep valid by pushing a refresh whenever a value escapes, and each query names a width R its answer may have. The SUM answer is the sum of the intervals, so meeting R at least read cost is knapsack (profit = read cost, weight = width, capacity = R); COUNT under a predicate has a greedy optimum. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and only the query-time cost of buying it down is optimized: the sources' upkeep, the choice of interval widths and any cost of imprecision are outside the model. The MIN rule's optimality proof is in an unread technical report. | Active |
| [THEORY-375](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-375.md) v2 | In one simulator evicting whole query-shaped cache regions, no replacement value function was best on every workload: a value based on distance from the current query beat LRU where queries clustered around a hot region or wandered with loops, while MRU was best on regular cyclic paths, by up to 2.3 times over the distance value and 9.6 times over LRU; none of the functions weighs what a region would cost to fetch again, and nothing is proved | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava and Tan (1996), [LIT-1113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1113.md), read in [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md). With semantic regions as the unit of eviction, Manhattan distance from the most recent query beat LRU at every query size on a skewed selection workload, and a directional variant was best or tied on random map paths (LRU within 1.06) and on lollipop paths circling a square five or more times; MRU won on a single circuit and on plain squares (Manhattan 2.29 and LRU 9.57 on the 32 × 32 square). The study is simulation only, with synthetic paths and no refetch cost in any value; it shows that the best forecast of reuse depends on the workload, not that semantic distance is a robust rule. | Active |
| [THEORY-377](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-377.md) v2 | In Olston, Loo and Widom's simulations, a rule that multiplies a cached interval's width by 1 + α on a pushed refresh with probability min{ρ, 1}, and divides it by 1 + α on a query's exact fetch with probability min{1/ρ, 1}, settled within 1% of the best fixed width on one random walk and within 5% over eight walk settings; on a 50-host network-traffic trace, restricted to exact copies, it almost matched a tuned adaptive cache-or-not rule, and with a 50-value cache, where queries tolerated imprecision, it cost less; that it converges to the best width is argued, not proved | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The rule treats a pushed refresh as "too narrow" and a fetch as "too wide", weighted by ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and needs no measurement of update rates, query rates or precision demands. Within 1% of the best fixed width on one random walk and within 5% over eight settings; with α = 1 and thresholds it tracked a 50-host traffic trace. With every copy forced exact it decided cache-or-not as well as an adaptive exact-caching rule, and did better where imprecision was allowed, except with a small cache. Convergence is argued from the balance condition only, all evidence is the authors' simulation, and there is no worst-case guarantee. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
| [THEORY-382](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-382.md) v2 | When a web server keeps each page fragment either cached and invalidated by updates or stored and refreshed after them, materializing trades staleness for response time, and in one synthetic simulation with fixed costs a periodic greedy that moves a capped number of fragments between the two, to keep the share of fresh fragments served above a set threshold, tracked that threshold by the authors' reading of its curves, answered faster than caching alone and recovered from overload by materializing everything; no bound on its distance from the best plan is shown | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2003), [LIT-1105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1105.md), read in [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md). Quality of Data is the share of fresh fragments in served pages; OVIS(θ) estimates per fragment the change in response time (hits and misses against refresh load) and in QoD from switching policy, and each period greedily switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments to spend a QoD surplus on speed or buy back a deficit. The paper asserts the greedy step is best under the cap and proves nothing; the evidence is one simulator with uniform costs and no comparison with an optimum. The reading the evidence does not support: that this is a joint cost model of build, upkeep, staleness and savings. Staleness is a user-set threshold, not a price, and switching and storage are free. | Active |
| [THEORY-383](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-383.md) v2 | On one Apache and Informix server answering cheap indexed selections over 1000 pages, a page whose query result was stored in the DBMS and refreshed on every update answered more slowly than one recomputed on each request at five or more updates per second, which the authors explain by reading the stored result costing about as much as recomputing it and its refresh loading the same DBMS, while a finished page stored at the web server and rewritten on every update answered 10 to 230 times faster than either | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2000), [LIT-1118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1118.md), read in [NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md). Three ways to serve a database-generated page under online updates, with no stale reads allowed: compute on request, store the query result in the DBMS, or store the finished page at the web server. A cost model sums access and update costs by frequency; the per-page selection problem is stated and not solved. On their testbed the page stored at the web server won at every load, and the result stored in the DBMS lost to recomputation at five or more updates per second. The reading the evidence does not support: that storing an answer pays whenever it is reused enough. Where it is stored decided the outcome, and the generalization to other systems is the authors' expectation, not a measurement. | Active |
| [THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md) | When a cached interval of width W is kept valid by its source, which pushes a refresh at cost C_vr whenever the value leaves it, and queries fetch the exact value at cost C_qr whenever it is too wide, and the chances of the two per step go as 1/W² and as W, the expected refresh cost is least at W* = (ρK₁/K₂)^(1/3) with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, where ρ times the chance of a pushed refresh equals the chance of a fetch | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The cost rate Ω(W) = C_vr·K₁/W² + C_qr·K₂·W is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr. The minimum is calculus on assumed forms. P_qr ∝ W follows exactly from uniform precision demands; P_vr ∝ 1/W² comes from a Chebyshev bound on a random walk used as an estimate, and the paper's simulation of a random walk measured both proportionalities. Staleness here is priced as refresh traffic: the source guarantees validity, so a stale read is imprecise but never wrong, and there is no build cost and no cost of a wrong or imprecise answer. | Active |

| [THEORY-654](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-654.md) | For full-state linear-quadratic regulation of a single-input plant, the return-difference identity keeps the sensitivity at or below 1 at every frequency, so the loop tolerates any gain increase, a gain cut to one half and at least 60° of phase error for any Q ≥ 0 and r > 0; the guarantee does not carry over when the state is replaced by an observer's estimate | Başar, Meyn & Perkins (2020), [LIT-051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-051.md), graduate course notes read in full in [NOTE-062](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-062.md), with every worked example recomputed. §10.6 derives \|1 + L(jω)\|² = 1 + \|P(jω)\|²/r ≥ 1 for the full-state loop, hence \|S\| ≤ 1 and the classical margins. It does not say that the finitely many pieces are few: exact solution is exponential in the worst case, and the infinite-horizon value may have infinitely many facets. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1396](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1396.md) | Mukhopadhyay and colleagues present static coverage models for emergency response as moving from deterministic models that treat a facility as always available, through multiple coverage as a partial hedge against busy stations, to probabilistic models that represent station availability explicitly, beginning with the maximum expected covering and maximum availability models | Mukhopadhyay et al. (2020), [LIT-2107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2107.md), read in part in [NOTE-1583](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1583.md) (§6.1 and Table 1). An account of how the review organizes the coverage literature, not of any model's correctness; the reader proposed none, since the part read is a taxonomy, and this one is limited to what that taxonomy states. Proposed until the owner judges whether a review's ordering of a literature is worth an account at all. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1401](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1401.md) | Bogetoft and Hougaard hold that an organization's measured technical inefficiency can be a rational choice of on-the-job slack traded against profit, so that under price-based or restriction-based control a rational unit still uses an efficient underlying plan, and its observed inputs reveal partial information about how it values the different kinds of slack | Bogetoft and Hougaard (2001, revised 2002; J. Productivity Analysis 2003), [LIT-2096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2096.md), read in part in [NOTE-1576](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1576.md). Proposed: the propositions were read as stated, without checking their proofs; the parameterized aggregators were skimmed and the applications not read; and there is no application to data. That inefficiency can be a choice is the paper's premise, argued, not shown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1402](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1402.md) | Akitaya, Demaine, Horiyama, Hull, Ku and Tachi prove that deciding whether a crease pattern can fold rigidly from flat is NP-hard: weakly when every crease must fold, and strongly when creases are optional | Akitaya et al. (2020), [LIT-2071](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2071.md), read in [NOTE-1579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1579.md) (model and main text in full, reduction gadgets skimmed). Proposed: the gadget constructions behind Theorems 15 and 16 were not checked line by line. It does not say that the problem is in NP in general, which is open, or anything about the mechanics of folding a real sheet. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1405](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1405.md) | Kinoshita and Ohsaki show that a bistable compliant truss mechanism, whose second stable state comes from snap-through stopped by contact with an obstacle, can be converted into a single-piece frame mechanism with the same function by optimizing thin pseudo-joints at its former pin joints under a strain cap, without lumping deformation into a point hinge | Kinoshita and Ohsaki (2009), [LIT-2029](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2029.md), read in full in [NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md). Proposed: the conversion is shown on one seven-node example, in simulation, with equivalence judged by overlaid force–displacement curves. It does not say that the frame is bistable without the obstacle, that the method finds frames without a truss to start from, or that a fabricated frame behaves as computed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1407](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1407.md) | Gopalan, Kolaitis, Maneva and Papadimitriou show that, for Boolean constraint languages with constants, deciding whether two solutions are joined by single-variable flips through solutions is either in polynomial time with components of linear diameter or PSPACE-complete with components of possibly exponential diameter, according to a property of the language that properly contains Schaefer's tractable classes and does not follow the boundaries of Boolean clones, a boundary Schwerdtfeger later corrected slightly toward the hard side | Gopalan et al. (2009), [LIT-2114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2114.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1584.md), with Schwerdtfeger's correction (2014), [LIT-2027](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2027.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1613.md). Proposed: the hard side's proofs were read only in outline, the SIAM version was not compared, and Schwerdtfeger's own proofs were not read. The lead added the work, not A. It does not say that algebra is irrelevant to navigation (polymorphisms do make every Schaefer language easy to navigate), nor anything about non-Boolean domains, other move sets or resource budgets. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1410](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1410.md) | Siemroth shows that when an agent privately knows its organization's spending needs and gains from spending above them, a principal who commits in advance does weakly better by letting the agent roll over some share of unused funds than none, effective only when the share exceeds the agent's marginal gain from misuse and sometimes best below full roll-over, while auditing only spending above a threshold under a punishment large enough that it is never imposed | Siemroth (SSRN 2021; IER 2024), [LIT-2103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2103.md), read in [NOTE-1594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1594.md) from the February 2022 working paper. Proposed: the results are the paper's propositions, whose proofs (in the appendix) were not read, and the version of record, which may differ, was not reached. Within the model they are stated for two periods, risk-neutral parties and uniform needs; the threshold audit holds in year 2 and in year 1 absent saving, an interval rule otherwise. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1412](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1412.md) | Guigues, Kleywegt and Nascimento propose that a per-station steady-state Markov-chain preparedness metric, used inside a one-step integer program for ambulance selection and reassignment, gives a real-time EMS policy whose mean allocation cost is lower than nine published dispatch policies in most simulated Rio de Janeiro configurations | Guigues, Kleywegt and Nascimento (2026), [LIT-2066](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2066.md), read in part in [NOTE-1567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1567.md). Proposed: the metric and policies were read in full, but the comparison rests on a simulation with assumed allocation costs whose per-figure results were skimmed, in an unrefereed preprint. The account is about mean allocation cost in one city's simulated system; it does not say the policy beats approximate dynamic programming, which was not compared, or that it holds under heavy load, where the authors say the metric may be inaccurate. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1413](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1413.md) | Schwerdtfeger shows that Gopalan, Kolaitis, Maneva and Papadimitriou's connectivity dichotomies for Boolean constraint languages overlooked constraints in which a variable occurs twice, and that they hold once tight sets are replaced by safely tight ones, whose relations keep their component properties when variables are identified, which moves the boundary slightly toward the hard side | Schwerdtfeger (2014), [LIT-2027](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2027.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1613](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1613.md): the abstract, §1, the definitions and §3 through the restated theorems read, §4–5 not. Proposed: the extended structural expressibility proof (Lemma 3.4) was read only as amended, not in full. It does not include the trichotomy for connectivity the paper also proves, whose proof was not read, and it says nothing beyond Boolean domains with constants and single-flip moves. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1416](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1416.md) | Halfin and Whitt: in a many-server queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service, the probability that an arrival waits tends to a value strictly between zero and one exactly when the number of servers exceeds the offered load by a multiple of its square root, and the scaled number in system then tends to a diffusion that is a negative-drift Brownian motion above full occupancy and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process below it | Halfin and Whitt (1981), [LIT-2085](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2085.md), unread, as reported by the tutorial of van Leeuwaarden, Mathijsen and Zwart (2019), [LIT-2059](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2059.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1577.md) (§§1, 2.1, 3, 4). The tutorial states both results in formulas and attributes them to Halfin and Whitt, without their proofs. Proposed until the original is read. It does not say that capacity sized to mean demand is wrong in every regime, nor that the headroom is idle: utilization tends to one. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1421.md) | Liebman and Mahoney hold that when an organization's budget expires at year-end and the value of its spending is uncertain, it holds a precautionary buffer through the year and spends it on low-value projects at the deadline, so that spending spikes and quality drops at year-end, and that letting unused funds roll over, given the budget-setter's commitment not to claw them back, removes most of the waste | Liebman and Mahoney (NBER 2013; AER 2017), [LIT-2028](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2028.md), read in [NOTE-1553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1553.md). Proposed: the model derives the mechanism; the spike and the quality drop are shown in US federal procurement only, the quality drop on rated I.T. projects only; the rollover effect on volume rests on one agency's authority, its effect on quality on one project; and the title's most of the waste is a calibrated welfare share, not a measurement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1426](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1426.md) | Hua, Luo, Swersey and Wen solve the spatial hypercube queueing model with server-specific service rates exactly, through a birth–death process and an equivalent reformulation whose iteration converges to the stationary distribution at a geometric rate | Hua, Luo, Swersey and Wen (2026), [LIT-2111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2111.md), read in part in [NOTE-1618](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1618.md) (§1, the model statement, the TOUR paragraph and the comparison of §5). Proposed: the extension and the geometric convergence are stated in the abstract and introduction, but the proof was not read. The reported speed-ups against a sparse solver, simulation and Larson's own method are not part of the account and were not checked against the tables. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1433](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1433.md) | Krishnakumar and Suresh show that compliant mechanisms can be designed by topology optimization without pseudo-densities, by removing material where the topological derivative of a mutual-to-weighted-input-and-output strain-energy objective is lowest, which yields designs without point hinges and lets one parameter trade geometric against mechanical advantage | Krishnakumar and Suresh (2015), [LIT-2099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2099.md), read in full in [NOTE-1582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1582.md) from a lab-posted manuscript, as a stand-in for Sigmund (1997). Proposed: hinge-freedom is shown by pictures of a handful of coarse-mesh designs, and the η trade-off on one example. It is the authors' account of their own method, not of Sigmund's; it does not say that the designs stay hinge-free under stress constraints or large deformation, or that they were built. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1434](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1434.md) | Raussen shows that for a concurrent PV program on shared resources of given capacities, a spare capacity computed from the program text bounds from below the connectivity of every space of executions to the target, so that spare capacity zero marks deadlocks, at least one excludes them, and at least two makes all executions equivalent | Raussen (2021; Computational Geometry 2023), [LIT-2073](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2073.md), read in part in [NOTE-1581](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1581.md), as the neighbour of Fajstrup, Goubault & Raussen 2006. Proposed: the proof of Theorem 4.3 was read, but Proposition 3.12's proof and the several-resource details of §§2.2.2–3.3 were not. It holds for linear PV programs with fixed capacities. It does not say anything about durations, energies or costs beyond feasibility, nor that the bound is tight in general. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1435](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1435.md) | Marsden and Zwart propose that quantitative resource theories are categories enriched in a commutative quantale, whose monoid combines the costs, probabilities or strengths of successive conversion steps and whose join selects the best alternative, with costly conversions as profunctors and closure under composition as a free internal monad | Marsden & Zwart (CSL 2018), [LIT-2054](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2054.md), read in full in [NOTE-1602](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1602.md). Proposed: the paper's proofs are sketches and were not checked further. It uses one quantale per theory and static resources. It does not say anything about several quantities at once beyond a product quantale, whose componentwise join loses a Pareto frontier of budgets, nor about costs that depend on the order of operations, nor about graded categories that keep every morphism with its grade. | Proposed |
